items.followUp: What are the main steps involved in defining a problem before writing a program?

rubric.why: Shows that the problem must first be understood.
rubric.description: Understand and identify the problem to be solved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the problem must be understood or clearly identified.

rubric.why: Inputs are part of a clear problem definition.
rubric.description: Identify the input data or information required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the input.

rubric.why: The required result must be made clear.
rubric.description: Identify the expected output or result.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the output.

rubric.why: Requirements and constraints make the problem statement specific.
rubric.description: State the requirements or constraints and express the problem clearly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning requirements, constraints, or a clear problem statement.

modelAnswer: Defining a problem means clearly understanding and stating what problem has to be solved.
Identify the input data needed to solve it.
Determine the output or result that is required.
Note the requirements and constraints so the problem is stated precisely.

items.followUp: Define data communication and name any four components of a data communication system.

rubric.why: Defines the purpose of data communication.
rubric.description: Define data communication as the exchange or transfer of data between devices.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition involving data exchange or transfer.

rubric.why: Sender and receiver are the communicating endpoints.
rubric.description: Name the sender and receiver as components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the sender and receiver.

rubric.why: The message is the information being communicated.
rubric.description: Name the message as a component.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the message or information being sent.

rubric.why: A communication system requires a route and rules for communication.
rubric.description: Name the transmission medium and protocol.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the medium/channel and protocol.

modelAnswer: Data communication is the exchange of data between two or more devices through a transmission medium.
The sender is the device that sends the data, and the receiver is the device that receives it.
The message is the data or information being communicated.
The transmission medium carries the data, and a protocol is the set of rules governing the communication.

items.followUp: Give two examples of sensitive information that encryption can help protect when using the internet.

rubric.why: Encryption helps keep communications private.
rubric.description: Explain that encryption protects privacy or confidentiality.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that information is kept private or confidential.

rubric.why: Credentials and financial details are common sensitive information online.
rubric.description: Give examples of sensitive information protected by encryption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example such as passwords or payment details.

rubric.why: Encryption makes data difficult for unauthorized people to understand.
rubric.description: Explain that encrypted data is unreadable to unauthorized people without the key.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the protection against unauthorized access or reading.

rubric.why: Encryption is important for common internet activities that involve sensitive data.
rubric.description: Connect encryption to safer online transactions or services.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking encryption to secure banking, shopping, or other online transactions.

modelAnswer: Encryption converts readable data into an encoded form that cannot be understood without the correct key.
It protects the privacy of everyday internet communications and helps prevent unauthorized people from reading them.
It helps safeguard sensitive information such as passwords and payment or banking details.
This makes activities such as online banking and shopping safer when information is sent over the internet.

items.followUp: Draw a flowchart to calculate the area of a square from its side length.

rubric.why: The flowchart needs a start and the cube's side length as input.
rubric.description: Show Start and input the side length S.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Start and an input step for the side.

rubric.why: The correct calculation and output determine the cube's volume.
rubric.description: Calculate V = S × S × S and display V, then end.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula and an output/end step.

modelAnswer: (Oval) START
(Parallelogram) Input side length S
(Rectangle) V = S × S × S
(Parallelogram) Display V
(Oval) END

items.followUp: What is the radix of the decimal number system, and how many digits does it use?

rubric.why: Radix means the base of a number system.
rubric.description: Define base or radix as the base of a number system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying radix as the base.

rubric.why: The radix gives the number of distinct symbols available in the system.
rubric.description: Explain that the radix is the number of distinct digits or symbols used, including zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the number of available digits/symbols.

modelAnswer: The base or radix of a number system is the number of distinct digits or symbols used to represent numbers in that system.
It includes zero; for example, the decimal system has radix 10 and uses the digits 0 to 9.

items.followUp: Why does a computer use binary digits to represent text, pictures, and sound?

rubric.why: Computer data is represented using binary digits.
rubric.description: State that data in a computer is represented in binary as 0s and 1s.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying binary digits 0 and 1.

rubric.why: Binary matches the two states used by electronic circuits.
rubric.description: Explain that computer circuits use two states, commonly represented as ON and OFF.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting binary representation to two electronic states.

modelAnswer: A computer represents all data as binary digits (bits), 0 and 1.
These digits correspond to the two states of electronic circuits, commonly represented as OFF and ON.

items.followUp: Using the commutative and associative laws, show that X · Y · Z = Z · Y · X.

rubric.why: Begins with the given expression and applies grouping consistently.
rubric.description: Write the given left-hand expression and use the associative law to regroup it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid associative regrouping of A · B · C.

rubric.why: The commutative law allows the factors to be exchanged.
rubric.description: Use the commutative law to change the order of factors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly applying commutativity.

rubric.why: The required right-hand side must follow from valid Boolean laws.
rubric.description: Complete the rearrangement and reach C · B · A.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each valid rearrangement step, up to 2 marks, ending with C · B · A.

modelAnswer: A · B · C = (A · B) · C  (associative law)
= C · (A · B)  (commutative law)
= C · (B · A)  (commutative law: A · B = B · A)
= (C · B) · A = C · B · A  (associative law)
Therefore, A · B · C = C · B · A.
